lessons.title: Winter pruning
lessons.html:
Winter pruning

Manipulation means the practices that shape the tree or vine and control how much it grows and bears: pruning, summer canopy work, thinning and training. Each crop and cultivar has its own rules, set by the farm's consultant. The foreman must understand the principles and make sure teams apply them consistently.

Why we prune

  • To keep the shape of the training system.
  • To balance growth and crop - a tree that carries too much fruit gives small fruit and weak buds for next year.
  • To open the canopy for light and spray penetration.
  • To renew fruiting wood.
  • To remove dead, diseased and damaged wood.

Types of cuts

A heading cut shortens a shoot and stimulates several shoots to grow below the cut. A thinning cut removes a shoot or branch completely at its origin and opens the canopy with less regrowth. Cuts should be clean, close to the bud or branch collar, and made with sharp tools.

Crop-specific basics

CropWhere the fruit isPruning focus
GrapesShoots from one-year-old woodSpur or cane pruning to a set number of buds
Apples and pearsSpurs on older wood and some one-year woodKeep good spurs, thin out crowded wood
Peaches and nectarinesOne-year-old shootsRenew fruiting shoots every year

Hygiene and safety

Disinfect tools as instructed when moving between blocks with disease. Remove prunings with disease and dispose of them. Workers must use secateurs and loppers safely, wear gloves and eye protection where required, and use ladders on firm ground, never on the top step.

lessons.title: Summer canopy management
lessons.html:
Summer canopy management

Summer work fine-tunes the canopy that winter pruning has set up.

In vineyards

  • Suckering and shoot thinning: removing unwanted shoots from the trunk and crowded shoots on cordons early in the season.
  • Shoot positioning: lifting wires and tucking shoots so the canopy stands upright and evenly spread.
  • Topping: cutting shoot tips that grow too long, to reduce shading and keep the rows passable.
  • Leaf removal: removing some leaves around bunches to improve air movement, reduce rot and improve spray coverage. Too much removal on the hot afternoon side can cause sunburn.

In orchards

  • Summer pruning: removing vigorous upright water shoots that shade the canopy.
  • Bending and tying: bending branches toward horizontal encourages fruit bud formation and reduces vigour, especially in apples and pears.
  • Removing competing leaders in young trees.

Timing

Summer work must be done on time. Shoot thinning done late wastes the plant's energy and makes the job slower. Leaf removal after berries are exposed to strong sun late in the season can cause sunburn. The consultant and the farm manager set the timing; the foreman plans labour so the work is done in the window.

Quality control

Count shoots per vine or check light in the canopy on sample plants per row. Compare with the standard. Give teams quick feedback while they are still in the row.

Worker safety in summer

Summer canopy work happens in heat. Provide drinking water and shade, schedule breaks, and watch for signs of heat stress. Check that workers do not enter blocks during the re-entry period after spraying shown on the spray record.

lessons.title: Crop load: thinning and plant growth regulators
lessons.html:
Crop load: thinning and plant growth regulators

Why manage crop load

A tree or vine has a limited amount of sugar to share. If it carries too many fruit, the fruit are small, ripen unevenly and next year's flower buds may be weak (alternate bearing). If it carries too few, yield is lost and fruit may be too large or soft. The aim is the right number of fruit, well spread, for the market size required.

Thinning methods

  • Blossom thinning: removing some flowers, by hand, mechanically or chemically as advised.
  • Chemical fruitlet thinning: registered products sprayed at a specific fruitlet size; weather strongly affects results, so the consultant decides.
  • Hand thinning: workers remove fruitlets to a set spacing or number per spur or branch. For table grapes, bunch thinning and berry thinning shape bunches to export specifications.

Supervising hand thinning

  1. Explain the standard: fruit per cluster, spacing in centimetres, which fruit to remove first (small, damaged, misshapen, badly placed).
  2. Demonstrate on a tree and let each worker try while you watch.
  3. Check sample trees per worker or row and count remaining fruit.
  4. Correct immediately; under-thinned trees cost money at harvest.

Plant growth regulators

Growers may use registered plant growth regulators to influence fruit set, size, colour, russeting or vigour - for example gibberellins for table grape berry size. These are agricultural remedies under Act 36 of 1947: apply only the registered product at the label rate, timing and crop, with the PPE the label requires.

Recording

Record the date, block, method, standard used, workers and sample counts. This helps the manager compare thinning results with harvest size.

Key points

  • Pruning keeps the training system, balances crop and growth and opens the canopy.
  • Know where fruit buds are on each crop before pruning.
  • Summer canopy work must be done in the right window.
  • Correct crop load gives good fruit size and prevents alternate bearing.
  • Use plant growth regulators only exactly as the label states.
